claims.text: In-situ high-resolution TEM heating can investigate the atomic-scale thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Increasing temperature induces atomic rearrangements in nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Increasing temperature induces localized phase separation in nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Thermally induced rearrangement and phase separation indicate reduced high-entropy stabilization at elevated temperatures.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a single-phase structure.
The preparation conditions ensure high configurational entropy in the AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The proposed intervention is incremental thermal annealing using an in-situ heating stage in a high-resolution TEM.
Heating enhances atomic diffusion and local atomic rearrangement in the nanoparticles.
Enhanced diffusion and rearrangement cause nanoscale defect formation or phase separation.
Elevated temperature increases atomic mobility sufficiently to overcome kinetic sluggishness.
Kinetic sluggishness supports the high-configurational-entropy state.
Thermally activated atomic rearrangements reduce mixing entropy.
Reduced mixing entropy induces subtle phase separation or precipitate nucleation.
TEM can reveal nanoscale precipitates and phase-dependent precipitation behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Above a temperature threshold, AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will develop dislocations, regionally distinct phases, or small precipitates.
These thermally induced defects or phases are absent at room temperature.
Room-temperature AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles exhibit a uniform, single-phase atomic structure with minimal defects.
The apparent transition temperature may depend on electron-beam effects and nanoparticle size.
Electron-beam effects or uncontrolled sample damage can produce artifacts at high temperature.
